RD-2 makes distance the refundable unit only for unexcused off-route segments on a metered trip, so everything turns on whether the single segment is exempt [RD-1][RD-2].

There is exactly one off-route segment, 12:27–12:35: 4.90 km driven where the optimal route covers 2.75 km, +2.16 km, up to 722 m off the corridor [F3]. Both advocates stipulate the ground for this segment as a general route choice by the rider, and RD-1 makes each segment the unit of review [F3][RD-1].

The rider's own message before the segment was a general route authorisation: the driver asked at 12:24 whether to take another way because the PIE jam was building, and the rider replied at 12:25 "随便你，哪条快走哪条，我赶时间" — leaving the route to the driver for the sake of speed [F8][F9][F10]. The trip was a metered RydeTAXI ride, 18.0 km driven against 15.1 km optimal (+2.9 km) and 30.1 min against a 20.6 min estimate, charged $38.58 [F1][F2][F7]. RD-2 makes distance the refundable unit only for unexcused off-route segments on a metered trip, so everything turns on whether the single segment is exempt [RD-1][RD-2].

There is exactly one off-route segment, 12:27–12:35: 4.90 km driven where the optimal route covers 2.75 km, +2.16 km, up to 722 m off the corridor [F3]. Both advocates stipulate the ground for this segment as a general route choice by the rider, and RD-1 makes each segment the unit of review [F3][RD-1].

The rider's own message before the segment was a general route authorisation: the driver asked at 12:24 whether to take another way because the PIE jam was building, and the rider replied at 12:25 "随便你，哪条快走哪条，我赶时间" — leaving the route to the driver for the sake of speed [F8][F9][F10]. That message is complete and timestamped, sent at 12:25, before the segment began at 12:27 [F10][F3][RD-5]. A general authorisation covers a route chosen to get to the destination, and the record shows no errand of the driver's own, no stop, and no loop that reaches nothing — no stop is measured in the segment and no driver-named detour place appears [F3][F8][F9][RD-5].

The rider's argument that the authorisation fails because the route was not in fact faster, read off the trip duration [F2], is not the test RD-5 sets: RD-5 defines the scope of a general authorisation by where the loop goes (an errand of the driver's own, a loop reaching nothing), not by a guarantee that the estimate is beaten; the presence of congestion on the corridor is corroborated, not contradicted, by the PIE speed band 2 record [F9][F2][F12][RD-5]. No RD-4 exemption is relied on, and none is available: there was no incident on the route, and a speed band alone cannot exempt a segment [F14][F12][RD-4].

Because the segment is exempt, there is no unexcused extra kilometre to refund: the sum is Σ(extra_km of non-exempt segments) = 0 × $1.4098/km = $0.00, the rate being this trip's distance fare ÷ distance km ($4.06 ÷ 2.88 km) [F3][F4][RD-2]. The waiting item of $0.11 for 0.4 min is a metered waiting unit that the rider does not seek, and the total of $38.58 stands [F5][F7][RD-3]. The driver has no prior upheld route dispute, so no account flag arises [F17][RD-6].

The exchange concerns traffic and route choice; there is no threat, intimidation, harassment, sexual remark or dangerous-driving allegation, so the screen is "none" [F8][F9][F11]. The route the driver took was not in fact faster: the whole trip ran 30.1 min versus the 20.6 min estimate (F2), so the rider's stated condition — whichever way is faster — was not met, and the general authorisation does not cover this loop.

No reasonable cause under RD-4 is made out: there were no traffic incidents near the route during the trip window (F14), and the only congestion record — PIE speed band 2 during 12:03–12:27 (F12) — overlaps an already cleared jam that the driver himself described at 12:24 as 'building up ahead' (F8); under RD-4(b) a band record alone cannot exempt a segment, and it does not speak to the replaced portion of the optimal route past 12:27.
The driver invoked the congestion excuse only in his written post-trip statement ('I went round'), not in any record that ties a justified reroute to the 12:27–12:35 segment (F11, F3).
The chat record is complete and every message is timestamped (F10), so the consent question can be decided on the record without resort to G12/G13 escalation.

The waiting fee billed is only $0.11 for 0.4 min (F5); it arises from the metered ride, and on the metre units it follows the ride — the refund sought is confined to the unexcused segment's distance, not to waiting.
The rider has no upheld route dispute in the last 90 days and the driver has none either (F16, F17), so no flag_account on the driver is sought; the request is confined to the money.

weaknesses: The rider's own message F9 ('随便你，哪条快走哪条') IS consent given before the segment (12:25 < 12:27), and RD-5 says a general route authorisation covers the route chosen to reach the destination — the driver will argue the 12:27–12:35 loop is exactly that, citing F8+F9.

Traffic fact F12 records PIE speed band 2 (10–19 km/h) during 12:03–12:27, which the driver will use with F8 to say a jam on the optimal corridor was real (RD-4(a)/(b)); though F14 shows no incident and RD-4(b) alone cannot exempt, a judge may read F12 as corroborating the driver's reason.

weaknesses: The strongest point against us is the size of the deviation: 18.0 km actual vs 15.1 km optimal, +2.9 km (+19%), and a 4.90 km segment driven where the optimal route covers 2.75 km, adding 2.16 km and reaching up to 722 m from the optimal route (F1, F3) — the other side will say that is too far from the corridor to be 'another way' and looks like a loop, not a route.
